newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Study says Indonesian elections a mere formality.
newsitem.headline: Study says Indonesian elections a mere formality.

text.p: A study by the independent Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) has found that Indonesia's election system is flawed and designed to favour the ruling Golkar party, the Jakarta Post reported on Saturday.
The newspaper quoted the report as saying all the laws and state institutions relating to the election were in the ruling party's favour. It said the laws also allowed manipulation and poll rigging.
"It is not surprising, therefore, that many people consider the general election as a mere formality and a waste of money," said the CSIS, which groups political scientists and economists.

"These worries have grounds because all the legislative instruments have been formulated by the government. In real politics, it's clear that almost all government officials are ex-officio executives of one of the contestants, Golkar," said the report.

"The election is a tool by which politicians from Golkar, the United Development Party (PPP) and the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) meet their vested interests. The election will not fulfill people's hopes for a better system," the CSIS said.
CSIS officials could not be reached for comment on Saturday.
The ruling Golkar, the Moslem-based PPP and the Christian-Nationalist PDI are the three political parties legally allowed to contest the May 29 general elections.

Golkar, in power for the last 30 years under President Suharto, is seeking to push its share of the vote to more than 70 percent from the 68 percent it won at the last polls in 1992. The PPP won 17 percent and the PDI 15 percent.

The report said Golkar had held a virtual campaign in the form of "cadre meetings" for the past five years, while the two minority parties were barred from electioneering except during the specified campaign period from April 27 to May 23.

A split in the PDI would buttress the already overwhelming superiority of Golkar, it said, as Golkar would increase its absolute majority in parliament and the PPP would gain more seats at the cost of the PDI.
The PDI split into two camps last year after Megawati Sukarnoputri, daughter of Indonesia's first president, Sukarno, was ousted from the party's leadership by a government-backed faction.
